h1: Heavy periods can be a sign of a bleeding disorder that runs in families.
lede: Answer a few questions about your periods, your bleeding, and your family. You'll get a summary to show your doctor, including which tests to ask for.
startNote: About 4 minutes. Your answers stay on this phone and are not sent anywhere. This check does not diagnose anything.
q_urgent: Right now, are you soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for more than 2 hours, or feeling faint or dizzy from bleeding?
q_days: How many days does your period usually last?
q_flood: With most periods, do you bleed through your pad or tampon onto your clothes or bedding?
q_impact: With most periods, do you miss school, work, or plans because of bleeding?
q_anemia: Has a doctor ever treated you for anemia or low iron?
h_anemia: For example, iron pills, an iron infusion, or a blood transfusion.
q_family: Has anyone in your blood family been diagnosed with a bleeding disorder?
h_family: For example, von Willebrand disease or hemophilia.
q_events: Have you ever bled much more than expected after any of these?
q_pbac: Think about your last period. How many of each did you use?
h_pbac: Match what you used to the pictures. Your best guess is fine, or skip.
i_flood: Times you leaked onto clothes or bedding
scoreHeavy: (100 or more counts as heavy bleeding)
q_other: Do any of these happen to you?
o_clots: I pass clots bigger than a coin
o_hourly: On heavy days I change pads or tampons every hour
o_nose: Nosebleeds that last longer than 10 minutes
o_bruise: Large bruises when I don't remember getting hurt
q_fam: Has your mother, sister, aunt, or grandmother ever had any of these?
h_fam: Bleeding disorders are often never named in families. These signs can point to one.
f_transfusion: A blood transfusion or heavy bleeding after childbirth
f_procedure: Heavy bleeding after surgery or a tooth pulled
f_hyster: Her uterus removed at a young age because of bleeding
urgBody: Heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting, or soaking a pad or tampon every hour for more than 2 hours, needs care today. Go to urgent care or an emergency room, or call 911 if you feel faint or short of breath.

r_flagT: Ask your doctor about bleeding disorder testing
r_flagB: Your answers match the screen doctors use to decide who should be tested for a bleeding disorder like von Willebrand disease. This does not mean you have one. Many people who screen positive do not, but testing is how you find out.
r_warnT: Your periods sound heavy. Talk to a doctor.
r_warnB: This screen did not flag a bleeding disorder, but heavy periods still deserve a checkup. Heavy bleeding often leads to low iron.
r_okT: This screen did not flag a bleeding disorder
r_okB: If your periods change, or any bleeding worries you, talk to a doctor anyway.

say: "My periods are heavy, and I screened positive on a bleeding disorder screening tool. I would like to be checked for anemia and for von Willebrand disease."
worth: A CBC and ferritin test if you feel tired, dizzy, or short of breath
shareTxt: Bleeding disorders run in families. If a sister, mother, or cousin has heavy periods, send her this check.
about: About this screen: in a study of 217 US women with heavy periods, it found 89 of every 100 women whose lab tests showed a bleeding problem, most often a platelet function defect, and 95 of 100 when combined with the blood loss chart (Philipp and colleagues, 2011). It flags many people who turn out not to have a disorder, by design, so fewer are missed.
footer: HerTruth uses a published screening tool that doctors use to decide who should be tested for a bleeding disorder (Philipp and colleagues, 2008 and 2011) and the Pictorial Blood Loss Assessment Chart (Higham, 1990). It is not a medical device and does not replace a doctor.

whyH: Heavy periods get treated. The cause often goes unchecked.
whyP1: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Estimates run from about 1 in 100 people to 1 in 10,000. Women are more likely to reach a doctor with it, because it shows up as heavy periods and heavy bleeding after childbirth (ASH, ISTH, NHF and WFH guideline, 2021).
whyP2: Many women are treated for low iron and never tested for the cause. The same guideline reports delays of 15 years or more between the first symptoms and a diagnosis. Knowing matters most before surgery, dental work and childbirth.

d1t: What counts as a heavy period?
d1p: Bleeding for more than 7 days, soaking a pad or tampon every hour for several hours in a row, or passing clots as big as a quarter. The Mayo Clinic lists these as signs of heavy menstrual bleeding.
d2p: Blood carries a protein called von Willebrand factor that helps platelets stick together and plug a cut. In this disease there is too little of it, or it does not work well, so bleeding lasts longer. It runs in families and affects men and women.

mf1q: Soaking through a pad every hour is just a normal heavy day.
mf1a: Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for several hours in a row is a sign of heavy menstrual bleeding, according to the Mayo Clinic.
mf2q: Bleeding disorders only affect boys and men.
mf2a: Von Willebrand disease affects women and men. Women are more likely to notice it, because it shows up as heavy periods.
mf3q: Low iron can happen before anemia shows up.
mf3a: In the CDC data our iron model was trained on, 221 of 461 iron-deficient girls and women still had normal hemoglobin.
mf4q: One normal blood test always rules out von Willebrand disease.
mf4a: Stress, illness, pregnancy and estrogen can raise von Willebrand factor for a while, so a doctor may repeat the test.
rdH: An anemia test alone misses many girls with low iron
rdP: Our iron model was trained on girls and women from the CDC's national NHANES survey, 2017 to March 2020, then tested on people it had never seen.
rdC1l: girls and women aged 12 to 49 with a ferritin test
rdC3l: of them still had normal hemoglobin
rdDotsH: The iron-deficient people in the held-out test set
rdNote: Real test-set counts. The model also raises more false alarms than hemoglobin alone, so a flag means order a ferritin test, not a diagnosis.
fqLede: Written for girls, women and parents first. If something here is unclear, write to us and we will fix the wording.
fq1q: Does this tell me whether I have von Willebrand disease?
fq1a: No. Only blood tests can show that. HerTruth tells you whether your answers match the screen doctors use to decide who should be tested. A positive screen is a reason to ask for testing.
fq2q: What counts as a heavy period?
fq2a: The Mayo Clinic lists these signs: bleeding for more than 7 days, soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several hours in a row, needing two pads at once, changing protection during the night, and clots as big as a quarter. A blood loss chart score of 100 or more also counts.
fq3q: I feel fine. Why was I flagged?
fq3a: The screen is built to catch as many people as possible, so it flags many whose tests come back normal. In a 2018 study of 248 girls with heavy periods, the tool caught 95% of bleeding problems but also flagged most girls without one (Zia and colleagues). A flag is a reason to test, not a result.
fq4q: Which tests should I ask for?
fq4a: A complete blood count (CBC) and ferritin, to check for anemia and low iron. For a bleeding disorder, von Willebrand factor antigen, von Willebrand factor activity and factor VIII. If results are low or unclear, a referral to a hematologist or hemophilia treatment center.
fq4b: Stress, illness, pregnancy and estrogen can raise von Willebrand factor for a while, so one normal result does not always settle it (Perez Botero, Hematology, 2024).
fq5q: Why does it ask about my family?
fq5a: Von Willebrand disease is inherited, and families often live with it for years without a name. Heavy periods, bleeding after childbirth, or a hysterectomy at a young age in your mother, sisters, aunts or grandmothers can point to it. Those answers go in your summary for the doctor.
fq6q: Is anything I type saved or sent?
fq6a: No. The check runs inside this page. There is no server, no database and no account. This device remembers only your language and your light or dark setting. If you use Find help, only the place you search for is sent to the map services.
fq7a: Yes. Heavy periods since the very first period are one of the signs doctors count when checking for a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease (Perez Botero, 2024). The screening tool was validated in adult women and later studied in teenagers. A parent or school nurse can go through it with a teen.
fq8a: Similar quizzes already exist in English. HerTruth is built for the girls and women they miss. Every translation is a first draft, and native-speaking clinicians will review them before public launch.
fq9q: What is the clinic tool for?
fq9a: School nurses and community clinics can enter a routine blood count and get an estimate of iron deficiency. Iron deficiency without anemia is common and is missed by hemoglobin alone. It does not screen for bleeding disorders.
fq10a: Please write to thefactorfoundation@gmail.com. Errors in the medical content, the wording or the translations are all worth reporting.

isP: Many girls and women are told heavy periods are normal. Sometimes the cause is a bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease, or low iron that a basic anemia test misses. Either one can go unnoticed for years. HerTruth helps you find out whether to ask a doctor for testing.
